title: Per-Tenant Budgets, Semantic Cache & Invalidation
scopeHtml: Scope: Controlling usage across customers, semantic-cache correctness and invalidating stale cached responses.

notes.title: Why budgets and caches exist in a multi-tenant LLM product
notes.html:
A tenant is one customer organisation that uses your product (a company with 500 employees is one tenant, not 500). A multi-tenant system serves many tenants from the same servers, the same prompts and the same model account. That sharing is what makes the product cheap to run, and it is also the source of two big problems.

Problem one is money. An LLM is billed per token (a token is a small chunk of text, roughly three quarters of an English word). Your provider bills YOU, one invoice, while you charge each tenant separately. If one tenant runs a loop that sends 50 million tokens overnight, your margin for the whole month on that tenant (and maybe on all tenants) disappears. A per-tenant budget is the control that says "this customer may use at most X, here is what happens at 80 percent, here is what happens at 100 percent".

Problem two is repeated work. Many users ask nearly the same question ("how do I reset my password?", "what is your refund policy?"). Paying the model to write the same answer 10,000 times is waste. A cache stores a finished answer and returns it for a repeat question. An exact cache only matches identical text. A semantic cache matches questions that mean the same thing even when worded differently, by comparing embeddings (a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of a text; similar meanings give vectors that point in similar directions).

The semantic cache is powerful and dangerous. If it wrongly says "these two questions are the same", the user gets a confident answer to a different question, possibly another tenant's private answer. And a cache that is right today is wrong tomorrow when the refund policy changes, so you need invalidation (removing or refreshing cached entries that are stale).

user request
   |
   v
[auth: who is the tenant?] --> [budget check] --> over? -> degrade or reject
   |                                  |
   v                                  v
[cache lookup, scoped to tenant] -> HIT: return cached answer (cost ~0)
   |
   MISS
   v
[LLM call] --> [record tokens against tenant budget] --> [store in cache with metadata]

Existing notes cover the big picture: see also "Caching and cost layers" and "Multi-tenancy and isolation" in 01_A1.md, and "Cost trade-offs" in 03_D1.md. This note goes deeper on the mechanics, the maths, the code and the failure modes of three things: budgets, semantic-cache correctness and invalidation.

Real products: Helicone, Portkey, LiteLLM proxy and Cloudflare AI Gateway all offer per-key or per-team spend limits and response caching in front of LLM providers; GPTCache is an open-source semantic cache library; Redis offers vector search that teams use as a semantic cache (verify current product names and features in each project's docs).

Analogy (after the explanation): a shared office building. Each company gets a metered electricity supply so one tenant cannot run up the shared bill (budgets). The front desk keeps a binder of answers to common visitor questions, but must check that the binder is for the right company and that the answers have not gone out of date (semantic cache and invalidation).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we have a rate limit, so we have a budget". A rate limit caps speed (requests per minute); a budget caps total spend over a period. You need both.
  • Treating the cache as only a cost feature. It is also a correctness and security surface: a wrong hit is a wrong answer or a data leak.
  • Forgetting that provider prompt caching (a provider discount for a repeated prompt prefix) is a different thing from your own response cache. Provider caching still runs the model; your cache skips it.

notes.title: Metering: counting tokens and turning them into money
notes.html:
You cannot budget what you do not measure. Metering means recording, for every request, who used how much of what.

What to record per request: tenant id, user id, feature name, model id, input tokens, output tokens, cached-input tokens (if the provider reports them), whether it was a cache hit, latency, and computed cost. Provider responses return a usage block (for Anthropic, the response has a usage object with input_tokens and output_tokens; verify the exact fields, including cache read and write counts, in the SDK docs).

The cost formula:

cost = input_tokens  * price_in_per_token
     + output_tokens * price_out_per_token
     + cached_read_tokens * price_cached_per_token   (if applicable)

Example (made-up prices, NOT real; verify current prices):
  price_in  = $3  per 1,000,000 tokens  = $0.000003 per token
  price_out = $15 per 1,000,000 tokens  = $0.000015 per token
  request: 2,000 input tokens, 500 output tokens
  cost = 2000 * 0.000003 + 500 * 0.000015
       = 0.006 + 0.0075
       = $0.0135
  A tenant sending 10,000 such requests per day = $135 per day = about $4,050 per 30 days.

Notice output tokens are usually priced several times higher than input tokens, so a cap on max_tokens (the output limit you send with each call) is itself a budget tool.

Estimate before, settle after. The true output size is unknown until the call finishes. So the budget system uses two numbers: an estimate before the call (input tokens you can count in advance, plus the max_tokens you allowed as a worst case) and the actual usage after the call. Section "Enforcing budgets" shows the reserve-then-settle pattern.

Use a price table, not hard-coded constants. Prices change and differ by model. Keep a versioned table keyed by model id and look prices up at write time; also store the raw token counts so you can recompute cost if a price was wrong (verify the current price list in the provider docs).

Units. Many teams budget in "credits" or "tokens" rather than dollars, so a model price change does not break contracts. Tokens are not comparable across models (a large model token is worth more than a small model token), so either budget in money or give each model a weight (for example a small model costs 1 credit per 1,000 tokens, a large model 10).

Failure patterns seen in production:

  • Cost computed from the request, not the response, so retries and failed calls are billed wrongly.
  • Tool-using agents make 5 to 30 model calls per user request; metering only the first call undercounts badly. Attribute every call in a loop to the same tenant and request id.
  • Streamed responses that the user cancels: tokens already generated are still billed by the provider, so count what was actually received.

Analogy (after): a taxi meter. It ticks as the ride happens, the final fare is only known at the end, but the driver wants to know at the start whether you can pay for the trip.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting only input tokens. Output tokens are often the larger part of the bill.
  • Ignoring that different models have different prices when summing "tokens used".
  • Storing only cost and not raw token counts, which makes price corrections impossible.
  • Metering at the API gateway only, missing background jobs and agent sub-calls that bypass it.

notes.title: Designing per-tenant budgets: limits, quotas and tiers
notes.html:
Three different controls get mixed up; separate them.

Control Caps Time window Typical action when hit
Rate limit requests or tokens per minute seconds to a minute HTTP 429 with Retry-After
Concurrency limit simultaneous in-flight requests instant queue or 429
Budget / quota total spend or tokens day, month, contract period warn, degrade, then block

Budget levels (a hierarchy). Budgets nest: platform total, then tenant, then team or project, then user, then feature. A request must pass every level. Example: tenant Acme has $2,000 per month; inside it the "support-bot" feature has $1,200 and each user has a daily cap of $5, so one employee cannot burn the team's allowance.

Soft and hard limits. A soft limit (say 80 percent) triggers an alert to the tenant admin and your account manager and may start gentle degradation. A hard limit (100 percent) stops or sharply restricts usage. Many contracts also allow overage: usage beyond the plan is allowed at a higher price, with a separate absolute ceiling to stop runaway loops.

What "degrade" can mean (cheaper than refusing):

  1. Route to a smaller, cheaper model (for example from claude-sonnet-5-5 to claude-haiku-5-5; model ids from the shared brief, verify against docs).
  2. Lower max_tokens and trim retrieved context.
  3. Serve only from cache (cache-only mode): answers for known questions still work, new ones are queued or refused.
  4. Move non-urgent work to a batch queue that runs at a discount or off-peak.
  5. Block with a clear message and a self-serve way to top up.
spend / budget
0%          80%                  100%               120% (absolute ceiling)
|-----------|--------------------|-------------------|
   normal      soft: alert +        hard: degrade/      kill switch:
               smaller model        block new requests  stop everything

Plans and pooling. Free tier: small fixed budget, small model only. Pro: larger budget, per-user caps. Enterprise: pooled team budget plus negotiated overage. Decide what resets (monthly) and what rolls over (prepaid credits often do not).

Reset logic is a bug source. Use the tenant's billing period, not the calendar month, if invoices differ. Store period start in UTC. A reset at midnight on a server in one time zone surprises a tenant in another. Never "reset" by deleting counters in a cron job that may run twice; instead key counters by period (for example budget:acme:2026-11) so a new period is simply a new key.

Showing the tenant their usage. A dashboard with usage by feature and by user, plus webhooks at 50, 80 and 100 percent, removes most support tickets and makes hard limits acceptable.

Analogy (after): a mobile data plan. You get a text at 80 percent, speeds are throttled after the limit instead of the line going dead, and you can buy a top-up.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering only a hard cutoff. A good answer includes soft alerts and graceful degradation.
  • One global limit for all tenants, so one noisy tenant starves the rest.
  • Resetting counters by a cron job that deletes keys (double runs, missed runs, time zone mistakes).
  • Forgetting per-user and per-feature levels inside a tenant, so one runaway script uses the whole tenant allowance.

notes.title: Enforcing budgets correctly: atomic counters and reserve-then-settle
notes.html:
The naive way is "read the spend, if under limit then call the model, then add the cost". Under concurrency this is a race condition: 100 requests arrive together, all read spend = $99 of a $100 budget, all pass, all call the model, and you overspend by 100 times. The fix is an atomic operation (one indivisible step that cannot be interleaved with another) in a shared fast store, usually Redis.

Reserve-then-settle, step by step:

  1. Estimate worst-case cost: counted input tokens plus max_tokens times the output price.
  2. Reserve that amount atomically: "add estimate to spend only if spend + estimate <= limit, else reject". One Lua script in Redis, or INCRBYFLOAT plus a check and roll back.
  3. Call the model.
  4. Settle: replace the reservation with the actual cost (add actual - estimate, which is usually negative, so you refund the unused part).
  5. If the call failed before the model ran, release the whole reservation. Do this in a finally block, otherwise failed calls leak reserved money until the tenant appears over budget while idle.
limit = 100.00, spent = 99.00
req A estimate 0.50 -> 99.50 <= 100 OK (reserved)
req B estimate 0.50 -> 100.00 <= 100 OK (reserved)
req C estimate 0.50 -> 100.50 >  100 REJECT
A finishes actual 0.20 -> settle: 100.00 + (0.20 - 0.50) = 99.70

Reserving a worst case makes the budget slightly conservative (some requests are rejected a little early). The alternative, allowing a small overshoot, is acceptable for soft budgets; for hard financial caps use reservation.

Python with Redis (a Lua script makes check-and-add atomic; redis-py is the standard client):

import redis

r = redis.Redis()  # connection settings from env in real code

# KEYS[1]=spend key, ARGV[1]=estimate (micro-dollars), ARGV[2]=limit
RESERVE = r.register_script("""
local spent = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
if spent + tonumber(ARGV[1]) > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 end
redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
return 1
""")

def call_with_budget(tenant, period, limit_micro, estimate_micro, do_call):
    key = f"budget:{tenant}:{period}"           # period in key => natural reset
    if RESERVE(keys=[key], args=[estimate_micro, limit_micro]) == 0:
        raise RuntimeError("budget exceeded")    # map to HTTP 402/429 in the API layer
    try:
        result, actual_micro = do_call()         # returns answer and real cost
        r.incrby(key, actual_micro - estimate_micro)  # settle (usually refunds)
        return result
    except Exception:
        r.decrby(key, estimate_micro)            # release the reservation
        raise
# prints nothing; raises when the reserve script returns 0

Money is stored as integer micro-dollars (1 dollar = 1,000,000 micro-dollars) because floating point sums drift.

Kotlin with Lettuce (a common Redis client for the JVM; the same Lua script text):

import io.lettuce.core.ScriptOutputType
import io.lettuce.core.api.sync.RedisCommands

const val RESERVE_LUA = """
local spent = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
if spent + tonumber(ARGV[1]) > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 end
redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
return 1
"""

fun <T> callWithBudget(
    redis: RedisCommands<String, String>,
    tenant: String, period: String,
    limitMicro: Long, estimateMicro: Long,
    doCall: () -> Pair<T, Long>,
): T {
    val key = "budget:$tenant:$period"
    val ok = redis.eval<Long>(
        RESERVE_LUA, ScriptOutputType.INTEGER,
        arrayOf(key), estimateMicro.toString(), limitMicro.toString(),
    )
    check(ok == 1L) { "budget exceeded" }
    try {
        val (result, actual) = doCall()
        redis.incrby(key, actual - estimateMicro)   // settle
        return result
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        redis.decrby(key, estimateMicro)            // release
        throw e
    }
}

Java with Jedis (verify the exact eval overload in your Jedis version):

import redis.clients.jedis.Jedis;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public final class BudgetGate {
    static final String RESERVE_LUA =
        "local spent = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') " +
        "if spent + tonumber(ARGV[1]) > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 end " +
        "redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) return 1";

    public record Result<T>(T value, long actualMicro) {}

    public static <T> T call(Jedis redis, String tenant, String period,
                             long limitMicro, long estimateMicro,
                             Supplier<Result<T>> doCall) {
        String key = "budget:" + tenant + ":" + period;
        Object ok = redis.eval(RESERVE_LUA, List.of(key),
                List.of(String.valueOf(estimateMicro), String.valueOf(limitMicro)));
        if (!Long.valueOf(1).equals(ok)) throw new IllegalStateException("budget exceeded");
        try {
            Result<T> r = doCall.get();
            redis.incrBy(key, r.actualMicro() - estimateMicro); // settle
            return r.value();
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            redis.decrBy(key, estimateMicro);                   // release
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

Production notes:

  • Redis is a fast counter, not the system of record. Write each usage event to a durable log (Kafka, a database table) and reconcile; invoices come from the log.
  • If Redis is down, decide fail-open (keep serving, risk overspend) or fail-closed (block). Many teams fail open with a small local in-memory cap per instance plus an alert.
  • Counters per tenant and per period expire with EXPIRE set a few days after the period ends.

Analogy (after): holding a restaurant table with a card deposit. You put a deposit down first (reserve), eat, then the bill is settled and the unused deposit is returned.

Common interview traps.

  • Check-then-act without atomicity, which allows overspend under concurrency.
  • Never releasing reservations on error, so idle tenants look over budget.
  • Using floats for money.
  • Claiming Redis alone is billing-grade; the durable usage log is.

notes.title: Fairness and noisy neighbours: rate limits, queues and priorities
notes.html:
A noisy neighbour is a tenant whose heavy use slows or blocks others. Budgets protect money; they do not protect capacity. Your provider gives YOU an account-level limit (requests and tokens per minute, which depend on your plan; verify in the provider docs). If tenant A burns 90 percent of it in a burst, tenants B to Z get 429 errors even though everyone is under budget.

Tools, from simplest up:

  1. Token bucket per tenant. A bucket holds up to capacity tokens (here "tokens" means permits, not LLM tokens) and refills at rate per second. Each request takes permits; empty bucket means wait or 429. It allows short bursts but caps the average.
capacity = 60 requests, refill = 1 per second
t=0   bucket 60, burst of 60 requests -> all pass, bucket 0
t=1   bucket 1  -> 1 request passes
average speed is capped at 1/s, bursts up to 60 allowed
  1. Limit LLM tokens per minute, not only requests. One request with a 100,000-token document costs far more capacity than a short chat message. Count estimated tokens against a tokens-per-minute bucket.
  2. Weighted fair queuing. Each tenant has its own queue; the dispatcher takes from tenants in rotation weighted by plan (enterprise weight 5, free weight 1). Spare capacity flows to whoever needs it, but nobody is starved.
  3. Priority lanes. Interactive chat gets a high-priority lane and a reserved slice of provider capacity (for example 70 percent); batch summarisation uses the leftover. When the provider returns 429, batch backs off first.
  4. Admission control by queue depth. If the queue wait would exceed the latency target, return 429 quickly with Retry-After; a fast failure beats a 60-second hang.
  5. Isolation tiers. Large tenants may get a dedicated provider key or dedicated capacity so their load cannot affect others (and their spend is clean on the invoice).

Provider 429s: when the provider rejects you, do exponential backoff with jitter (wait 1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... each randomised) and respect any Retry-After header. Do not retry in a tight loop; that makes the shortage worse. Also use a circuit breaker (stop calling for a short period after repeated failures).

Production incident pattern: a tenant's nightly import triggers 20,000 summarisation calls at 09:00 local time. The token bucket for that tenant empties after the first burst; the rest queue in the batch lane, interactive traffic is untouched, spend alerts fire at 80 percent, and the tenant admin receives a webhook. Without these controls the same event shows up as everyone's chatbot timing out and a surprise $8,000 invoice.

Analogy (after): a motorway with a bus lane. Lorries (batch jobs) are allowed, but the bus lane (interactive users) stays moving, and a ramp meter limits how fast each on-ramp feeds cars in.

Common interview traps.

  • Rate limiting by request count only, ignoring wildly different token sizes.
  • A single FIFO queue shared by all tenants, so one tenant's burst delays everyone.
  • Retrying 429s immediately without jitter (a retry storm).
  • Forgetting that the provider limit is shared by all tenants, so your per-tenant limits must sum to less than the account limit (or be dynamic).

notes.title: Semantic cache: how it works step by step
notes.html:
An exact cache key is a hash of the whole request. "How do I reset my password" and "how can I reset my password?" produce different hashes, so exact caches miss most paraphrases. A semantic cache matches by meaning.

Mechanism:

  1. Normalise the query (trim, lowercase for matching only; keep the original for display).
  2. Embed it: call an embedding model that turns text into a vector, for example 768 or 1,536 numbers (the size depends on the model).
  3. Search the vector store for the nearest stored query vectors, restricted to the correct scope (tenant, model, prompt version, language; see the scoping section).
  4. Compare using cosine similarity (a number from -1 to 1 that measures how aligned two vectors are; 1 means same direction). Higher means more similar meaning.
  5. Decide: if the best score is at or above the threshold (say 0.92), return the cached answer; otherwise it is a miss.
  6. On a miss, call the LLM, then store (query vector, query text, answer, metadata).

Cosine similarity maths, shown on a tiny 2-dimensional example (real vectors have hundreds of dimensions):

a = (3, 4)   b = (4, 3)
dot(a,b)  = 3*4 + 4*3 = 24
|a| = sqrt(9+16) = 5      |b| = sqrt(16+9) = 5
cosine = 24 / (5*5) = 0.96

Python with numpy (the lookup is brute force; in production use FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant or Redis vector search):

import numpy as np

class SemanticCache:
    def __init__(self, embed, threshold=0.92):
        self.embed = embed            # function: str -> np.ndarray (unit length)
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.items = []               # list of (vector, scope, query, answer)

    def get(self, query, scope):
        q = self.embed(query)
        best, best_score = None, -1.0
        for vec, sc, text, answer in self.items:
            if sc != scope:           # hard filter first: never compare across scopes
                continue
            score = float(np.dot(q, vec))   # cosine, because vectors are unit length
            if score > best_score:
                best, best_score = answer, score
        return best if best_score >= self.threshold else None

    def put(self, query, scope, answer):
        self.items.append((self.embed(query), scope, query, answer))
# get() returns the cached answer string, or None on a miss

Kotlin (plain math; the embedding function would call your embedding API):

data class Entry(val vec: FloatArray, val scope: String, val query: String, val answer: String)

class SemanticCache(private val embed: (String) -> FloatArray, private val threshold: Float = 0.92f) {
    private val items = mutableListOf<Entry>()

    private fun dot(a: FloatArray, b: FloatArray): Float {
        var s = 0f
        for (i in a.indices) s += a[i] * b[i]   // unit-length vectors: dot == cosine
        return s
    }

    fun get(query: String, scope: String): String? {
        val q = embed(query)
        val best = items.filter { it.scope == scope }          // scope filter first
            .maxByOrNull { dot(q, it.vec) } ?: return null
        return if (dot(q, best.vec) >= threshold) best.answer else null
    }

    fun put(query: String, scope: String, answer: String) {
        items += Entry(embed(query), scope, query, answer)
    }
}

Java:

import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class SemanticCache {
    record Entry(float[] vec, String scope, String query, String answer) {}
    private final List<Entry> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Function<String, float[]> embed;
    private final float threshold;

    public SemanticCache(Function<String, float[]> embed, float threshold) {
        this.embed = embed; this.threshold = threshold;
    }

    private static float dot(float[] a, float[] b) {
        float s = 0f;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i] * b[i]; // unit vectors: cosine
        return s;
    }

    public Optional<String> get(String query, String scope) {
        float[] q = embed.apply(query);
        Entry best = null; float bestScore = -1f;
        for (Entry e : items) {
            if (!e.scope().equals(scope)) continue;           // never cross scopes
            float s = dot(q, e.vec());
            if (s > bestScore) { bestScore = s; best = e; }
        }
        return (best != null && bestScore >= threshold)
                ? Optional.of(best.answer()) : Optional.empty();
    }

    public void put(String query, String scope, String answer) {
        items.add(new Entry(embed.apply(query), scope, query, answer));
    }
}

Cost and latency of the cache itself: every lookup pays one embedding call (a few milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, and a very small cost compared with a chat completion; verify for your embedding model) plus a vector search. On a miss you have added that overhead on top of the LLM call, so a cache with a 5 percent hit rate can cost more than it saves. Rough break-even: if a hit saves cost C_llm and a lookup costs C_lookup, the cache pays off when hit_rate * C_llm > C_lookup. With C_llm = $0.0135 (from the earlier example) and C_lookup about $0.00001, break-even hit rate is 0.00001 / 0.0135 = 0.07 percent on cost; latency, not money, is usually the real constraint.

Real products: GPTCache (open source), Redis semantic caching features (LangChain and RedisVL integrations), Portkey and LiteLLM gateway caching modes (verify current options in their docs).

Analogy (after): a librarian who recognises that "books about cooking Italian food" and "Italian recipe books" point to the same shelf, but has to be careful not to send you to the shelf about Italian history.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a semantic cache is "just a key-value cache with fuzzy keys". It is a nearest-neighbour search plus a decision rule, and the decision rule is where bugs live.
  • Ignoring the embedding and search overhead on cache misses.
  • Using a threshold from a blog post instead of calibrating on your own data.
  • Searching first and filtering by tenant afterwards (leaks and wastes top-k slots); filter first or use per-scope indexes.

notes.title: Semantic cache correctness: preventing wrong hits
notes.html:
A false hit is when the cache returns an answer for a question that is similar in wording but different in meaning or context. This is the central correctness risk. Embedding similarity measures topical closeness, not "would the same answer be correct".

Classic false-hit examples (all score high on cosine similarity):

  • "How do I enable two-factor authentication?" vs "How do I disable two-factor authentication?" (one word flips the meaning).
  • "What is the refund policy for annual plans?" vs "...for monthly plans?"
  • "Is Python 3.9 supported?" vs "Is Python 3.12 supported?"
  • "Show my invoices" asked by user 1 and user 2 (the same words, different data).
  • "What is the current price of X?" yesterday and today.

Defences, layered (use several, not one):

1. Scope everything in the key, before similarity. Similarity only ranks candidates inside an exact-match scope: tenant id, model id, prompt version, system-prompt hash, language, locale, retrieval index version, tool set version, and a permission hash (the set of documents or roles the asker can see). Two users with different access rights must never share an entry. See the next section.

2. Do not cache personalised or tool-dependent answers. If the answer depended on a tool call (order lookup, account balance) or on the user's identity, do not store it in a shared semantic cache. Classify requests as cacheable or not using the route (FAQ intent only), a flag set by the prompt pipeline, or a small classifier.

3. Threshold calibration with data. Collect real query pairs, label each "same intent: yes/no", compute their cosine scores and choose the threshold where false-hit rate is within your tolerance.

score band      pairs   truly-same   false hits if you accept this band
0.98 - 1.00      400       399           1   (0.25%)
0.95 - 0.98      300       285          15   (5%)
0.92 - 0.95      250       200          50   (20%)
0.88 - 0.92      300       150         150   (50%)
Accepting >= 0.95: 700 pairs, 16 false = 2.3% false-hit rate. Accepting >= 0.92: 950 pairs, 66 false = 6.9%.

The numbers above are an illustration of the method, not real measurements. Pick the threshold from your own table, and set it per domain: a legal or medical assistant may need 0.98 or no semantic cache at all, while a trivia FAQ may accept 0.90. Thresholds depend on the embedding model; changing the model invalidates every calibrated threshold and every stored vector.

4. Verify before serving (two-stage hit). After a candidate passes the threshold, run a cheap check that the two queries have the same intent:

  • A small LLM judge call (a "verifier") given both questions: "Would the same answer be correct for both? yes/no." Cheaper than the full answer but not free.
  • Or a cross-encoder / reranker model that scores the pair directly (more accurate than comparing separate embeddings).
  • Or rule checks for the dangerous parts: compare numbers, versions, negations (not, disable), named entities and dates extracted from both queries; any difference means miss.

5. Store the original question with the answer and return metadata (cache age, source). A UI that says "answered from our help centre, updated 3 days ago" makes mistakes less harmful and debugging easier.

6. Canary and shadow testing. On a small fraction of hits (1 to 5 percent), also compute the fresh LLM answer in the background and compare it with the cached one (judge or embedding similarity). Track the disagreement rate as a live false-hit estimate and alert when it rises. This is the only way to know the real error rate of the cache in production.

7. Per-route cache policy. Read-only knowledge Q&A: enabled. Anything with side effects (send an email, create a ticket): never cached. Deterministic parameters: the cached answer is only valid for the same temperature, max_tokens and output format; include them in the scope or bypass the cache when they differ.

Code sketch of the two-stage decision (similarity then rule check), Python:

import re

def numbers_and_flags(text):
    nums = set(re.findall(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)*", text))
    negations = {w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower())
                 if w in {"not", "no", "never", "disable", "disabled", "without", "cannot"}}
    return nums, negations

def safe_hit(query, cached_query, score, threshold=0.93):
    if score < threshold:
        return False
    return numbers_and_flags(query) == numbers_and_flags(cached_query)
# safe_hit("enable 2FA", "disable 2FA", 0.97) -> False (negation words differ)

Kotlin:

private val negWords = setOf("not", "no", "never", "disable", "disabled", "without", "cannot")

private fun signature(text: String): Pair<Set<String>, Set<String>> {
    val nums = Regex("""\d+(?:\.\d+)*""").findAll(text).map { it.value }.toSet()
    val negs = Regex("""[a-z']+""").findAll(text.lowercase()).map { it.value }
        .filter { it in negWords }.toSet()
    return nums to negs
}

fun safeHit(query: String, cachedQuery: String, score: Float, threshold: Float = 0.93f): Boolean =
    score >= threshold && signature(query) == signature(cachedQuery)
// safeHit("enable 2FA", "disable 2FA", 0.97f) == false

Java:

import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public final class HitGuard {
    private static final Set<String> NEG =
        Set.of("not", "no", "never", "disable", "disabled", "without", "cannot");

    private static List<Set<String>> signature(String text) {
        Set<String> nums = new HashSet<>();
        Matcher m = Pattern.compile("\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)*").matcher(text);
        while (m.find()) nums.add(m.group());
        Set<String> negs = Pattern.compile("[a-z']+").matcher(text.toLowerCase())
            .results().map(MatchResult::group).filter(NEG::contains).collect(Collectors.toSet());
        return List.of(nums, negs);
    }

    public static boolean safeHit(String q, String cachedQ, float score, float threshold) {
        return score >= threshold && signature(q).equals(signature(cachedQ));
    }
}

This rule check is a cheap filter, not a proof; it catches many classic flips but misses synonyms ("turn off"). Combine it with a verifier for high-risk routes.

Production failure patterns: a product launched with threshold 0.85 and saw "cancel my subscription" answered with the "upgrade my subscription" steps; a shared cache without tenant scope returned a competitor's pricing answer; a model upgrade changed answer style but old cached answers kept the old style for weeks.

Analogy (after): a pharmacist who sees two prescriptions that look nearly the same. Similar handwriting is not enough; the dose and the patient name must match exactly before handing over the medicine.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "raise the threshold" as the only fix. Thresholds trade hit rate for safety but cannot fix scope bugs or negation flips.
  • Caching answers that depend on the user or on tool results.
  • Not measuring the false-hit rate in production (no shadow comparison).
  • Forgetting that changing the embedding model, the prompt or the model silently makes old entries wrong.

notes.title: Cache keys and scoping: tenant, version and permissions
notes.html:
Think of every cache entry as having an exact-match part (the scope) and a fuzzy part (the query meaning). Only the fuzzy part is compared by similarity.

Scope fields and why each exists:

Field Prevents
tenant id cross-customer data leaks
permission/ACL hash (roles, document groups) showing restricted content to users who cannot see it
model id (and snapshot) style and quality changes after an upgrade
prompt/system version stale behaviour after prompt edits
retrieval index version or corpus version answers based on old documents
embedding model id comparing vectors from different spaces (meaningless scores)
language/locale wrong-language answers
generation params (temperature, format, max tokens) mismatched output shape
tool set version answers produced with different tool capabilities

A scope string, for example: t=acme|acl=7f3a|m=claude-sonnet-5-5|p=v14|idx=2026-11-03|emb=e3|lang=en. Hash it into a short key for use as a namespace or partition. Entries in other scopes are invisible to the search, so a prompt change simply creates a fresh empty cache (and old entries age out).

Data-layer enforcement. Put the scope in the vector store as indexed metadata and always send it as a filter, ideally enforced in a shared client library so a developer cannot forget it. pgvector: a WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND scope_hash = $2 before ORDER BY embedding <=> $3 LIMIT 1 (the <=> operator is cosine distance in pgvector; verify in docs). Qdrant: a payload filter. Redis: a tag field. For very sensitive tenants use a separate collection or database per tenant so a missing filter cannot leak.

Python pgvector query:

import psycopg  # psycopg 3; pgvector adapter registered on the connection

SQL = """
SELECT answer, 1 - (embedding <=> %(q)s) AS cosine
FROM semantic_cache
WHERE tenant_id = %(tenant)s AND scope_hash = %(scope)s
  AND expires_at > now()
ORDER BY embedding <=> %(q)s
LIMIT 1
"""

def lookup(conn, tenant, scope, qvec, threshold=0.93):
    row = conn.execute(SQL, {"q": qvec, "tenant": tenant, "scope": scope}).fetchone()
    return row[0] if row and row[1] >= threshold else None
# returns the cached answer or None

Kotlin (JDBC; the vector is passed as its text form [0.1,0.2,...] and cast, which pgvector accepts):

import java.sql.Connection

const val SQL = """
SELECT answer, 1 - (embedding <=> ?::vector) AS cosine
FROM semantic_cache
WHERE tenant_id = ? AND scope_hash = ? AND expires_at > now()
ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector
LIMIT 1
"""

fun lookup(c: Connection, tenant: String, scope: String, q: FloatArray, threshold: Double = 0.93): String? {
    val vec = q.joinToString(",", "[", "]")
    c.prepareStatement(SQL).use { ps ->
        ps.setString(1, vec); ps.setString(2, tenant); ps.setString(3, scope); ps.setString(4, vec)
        ps.executeQuery().use { rs ->
            return if (rs.next() && rs.getDouble(2) >= threshold) rs.getString(1) else null
        }
    }
}

Java:

import java.sql.*;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public final class CacheLookup {
    static final String SQL = """
        SELECT answer, 1 - (embedding <=> ?::vector) AS cosine
        FROM semantic_cache
        WHERE tenant_id = ? AND scope_hash = ? AND expires_at > now()
        ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector
        LIMIT 1""";

    public static String lookup(Connection c, String tenant, String scope,
                                float[] q, double threshold) throws SQLException {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
        for (int i = 0; i < q.length; i++) sb.append(i > 0 ? "," : "").append(q[i]);
        String vec = sb.append("]").toString();
        try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(SQL)) {
            ps.setString(1, vec); ps.setString(2, tenant);
            ps.setString(3, scope); ps.setString(4, vec);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                return (rs.next() && rs.getDouble(2) >= threshold) ? rs.getString(1) : null;
            }
        }
    }
}

Row-level security (Postgres RLS) can enforce tenant isolation in the database itself, so even a buggy query cannot read another tenant's rows (verify setup in the Postgres docs).

Do not mix cache entries across permission levels. In RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: the model answers from retrieved company documents), the answer is derived from documents the asker may see. If a manager's question produced an answer using an HR document, an intern asking the same words must not receive it. Either include the permission hash in the scope or cache only questions whose retrieved documents are all public within the tenant.

Privacy. Cached answers and stored queries may contain personal data. Apply the same retention, deletion (right to erasure) and encryption rules as for logs; support "delete all cache entries for tenant X" and "for user Y".

Analogy (after): a hotel with room-key cards. The key is cut for one room and one stay period; being near the right door (similar) must never be enough to open it.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting tenant id in the similarity text instead of as a hard filter. Embeddings are not an access-control mechanism.
  • Filtering after the top-k search, which can return zero valid results or leak through timing and ranking.
  • Omitting embedding model id from the scope, then comparing vectors from different models.
  • Ignoring permission differences inside one tenant.

notes.title: Cache invalidation: TTL, events and versions
notes.html:
Phil Karlton's joke applies: cache invalidation is one of the hard problems. Invalidation means making sure users do not get an answer that was right once but is wrong now. In an LLM product, answers go stale because of:

  1. The source content changed (a policy document, a price list, a product page).
  2. The model or prompt changed (new behaviour, new guardrails, a fixed bug in a prompt).
  3. The world changed (news, stock level, "today's date").
  4. The embedding model or index changed.
  5. A mistake was found in a cached answer (it was wrong or unsafe from the start).
  6. A tenant action (permissions revoked, data deletion request).

Strategies, from blunt to precise. Most systems combine them.

1. TTL (time to live). Every entry has an expiry (expires_at). Choose the TTL by how fast the underlying facts change and how bad a stale answer is: price and stock: seconds or no caching; policy FAQ: 1 to 7 days; stable how-to docs: 30 days. Add random jitter (for example TTL times a random factor between 0.9 and 1.1) so thousands of entries created together do not all expire together. TTL is simple but means up to one full TTL of staleness after a change.

2. Version-in-key (namespace bumping). Include prompt_version, model_id, index_version and corpus_version in the scope (previous section). Releasing a new prompt or re-indexing documents bumps the version; old entries are now unreachable and need no deletion, they just expire. This is O(1) invalidation and the safest method for global changes.

scope before: ...|idx=2026-11-03|p=v14   -> 40,000 entries
publish new docs, index version becomes 2026-11-05
scope after:  ...|idx=2026-11-05|p=v14   -> 0 entries (cold start)
old 40,000 entries are never read again; TTL cleans them up

The cost is a cold cache after every bump: hit rate falls to 0 and your LLM bill spikes briefly. Mitigate with gradual rollout, or cache warming (replay the top N most frequent questions through the new version in the background before switching traffic).

3. Event-driven (targeted) invalidation. Store with each entry the source document ids (and their versions or content hashes) that the answer used. When a document changes, a webhook or a change-data-capture stream (CDC: reading a database's change log) sends doc_changed(doc_id), and you delete entries that reference it. This needs a reverse index doc_id -> entry ids.

entry 91: query "refund window?" sources=[doc_17@v3, doc_22@v1]
event: doc_17 updated to v4
lookup reverse index doc_17 -> {entry 91, entry 135, ...} -> delete them

Python (a Redis set per document as the reverse index):

import redis
r = redis.Redis()

def store(entry_id, scope, answer, source_doc_ids, ttl_s):
    pipe = r.pipeline()
    pipe.hset(f"cache:{scope}:{entry_id}", mapping={"answer": answer})
    pipe.expire(f"cache:{scope}:{entry_id}", ttl_s)
    for d in source_doc_ids:
        pipe.sadd(f"doc_refs:{d}", f"cache:{scope}:{entry_id}")   # reverse index
    pipe.execute()

def on_doc_changed(doc_id):
    keys = r.smembers(f"doc_refs:{doc_id}")
    if keys:
        r.delete(*keys)                  # drop stale answers (vector index rows removed too in real code)
    r.delete(f"doc_refs:{doc_id}")
# store() writes entry + reverse links; on_doc_changed() deletes every entry that used the doc

Kotlin:

import io.lettuce.core.api.sync.RedisCommands

fun store(r: RedisCommands<String, String>, entryId: String, scope: String,
          answer: String, sourceDocIds: List<String>, ttlSeconds: Long) {
    val key = "cache:$scope:$entryId"
    r.hset(key, mapOf("answer" to answer))
    r.expire(key, ttlSeconds)
    sourceDocIds.forEach { r.sadd("doc_refs:$it", key) }        // reverse index
}

fun onDocChanged(r: RedisCommands<String, String>, docId: String) {
    val keys = r.smembers("doc_refs:$docId")
    if (keys.isNotEmpty()) r.del(*keys.toTypedArray())
    r.del("doc_refs:$docId")
}

Java:

import redis.clients.jedis.Jedis;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

public final class Invalidator {
    public static void store(Jedis r, String entryId, String scope, String answer,
                             List<String> sourceDocIds, long ttlSeconds) {
        String key = "cache:" + scope + ":" + entryId;
        r.hset(key, "answer", answer);
        r.expire(key, ttlSeconds);
        for (String d : sourceDocIds) r.sadd("doc_refs:" + d, key); // reverse index
    }

    public static void onDocChanged(Jedis r, String docId) {
        Set<String> keys = r.smembers("doc_refs:" + docId);
        if (!keys.isEmpty()) r.del(keys.toArray(new String[0]));
        r.del("doc_refs:" + docId);
    }
}

Detail to remember: the vector index and the metadata hash must be updated together; a deleted metadata entry with a surviving vector row creates a dangling hit. Prefer a store where both are the same row (pgvector table, Qdrant point).

4. Stale-while-revalidate (SWR). Serve the cached answer immediately even if slightly past a soft expiry, and refresh it in the background. Users get low latency and the entry is fixed for the next asker. Appropriate for low-risk content only, with a hard maximum age after which the entry is not served at all.

5. Validation on read. Store the source document versions with the entry; on a hit, do a cheap check ("are doc_17 and doc_22 still at v3 and v1?") against the document store, and treat a mismatch as a miss. This costs one fast lookup per hit but removes reliance on events arriving (events can be lost).

6. Manual and emergency purge. An admin API (and runbook) to purge by tenant, by scope, by entry id, or by a pattern of similar queries ("delete everything semantically near this wrong question"). Used when a bad answer is reported. Log who purged what.

7. Negative and error caching. Do not cache errors, refusals caused by transient failures or empty retrievals as if they were answers; or give them a very short TTL (seconds).

Time-sensitive questions. "What is today's date?", "latest news", "is the store open now?" depend on the clock. Detect time-sensitive intent (rules or a classifier, or a flag from the prompt) and skip the cache, or inject the current date into the scope (daily key).

Stampede (thundering herd) after invalidation. When a popular entry expires, 1,000 concurrent requests all miss and all call the LLM at once. Fixes: a per-key lock or single-flight (the first request computes, others wait for its result), refresh slightly before expiry, and jittered TTLs. Python single-flight with a Redis lock:

import time, uuid

def get_or_compute(r, key, compute, lock_ttl_s=30, wait_s=0.1, max_wait_s=10):
    val = r.get(key)
    if val is not None:
        return val
    token = str(uuid.uuid4())
    if r.set(f"lock:{key}", token, nx=True, ex=lock_ttl_s):   # I am the one who computes
        try:
            val = compute()
            r.set(key, val, ex=3600)
            return val
        finally:
            if r.get(f"lock:{key}") == token.encode():         # release only my own lock
                r.delete(f"lock:{key}")                        # (not atomic; use a Lua script in real code)
    deadline = time.time() + max_wait_s
    while time.time() < deadline:                              # others wait for the winner
        time.sleep(wait_s)
        val = r.get(key)
        if val is not None:
            return val
    return compute()                                           # fallback after waiting too long

Kotlin and Java: JVM services usually do single-flight in process with a ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> and computeIfAbsent, and use Caffeine's AsyncLoadingCache (which coalesces concurrent loads of the same key) for the local layer; across servers use the Redis lock above. Kotlin:

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap

class SingleFlight {
    private val inFlight = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>>()

    fun get(key: String, compute: () -> String): String {
        val future = inFlight.computeIfAbsent(key) {
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(compute)   // only the first caller starts the work
        }
        try { return future.get() } finally { inFlight.remove(key, future) }
    }
}

Java:

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public final class SingleFlight {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> inFlight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public String get(String key, Supplier<String> compute) throws Exception {
        CompletableFuture<String> f =
            inFlight.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(compute));
        try { return f.get(); } finally { inFlight.remove(key, f); }
    }
}

Real systems: CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly) use stale-while-revalidate and surrogate keys for targeted purge, the same ideas as above; Caffeine and Guava caches coalesce loads; RAG platforms re-embed only changed chunks using content hashes.

Analogy (after): supermarket shelves with "use by" dates (TTL), a recall notice for one batch (event-driven purge), a new packaging design that means all old stock is pulled and replaced (version bump), and staff restocking a popular item before the shelf is empty (refresh ahead, no stampede).

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on TTL alone for content that must change immediately (a corrected legal policy).
  • Bumping versions with no cache warming plan, then being surprised by a cost and latency spike.
  • Event-driven invalidation without a TTL backstop; lost events leave entries stale forever.
  • Deleting the metadata but not the vector row (or the reverse), leaving dangling or orphan entries.
  • Forgetting that purging the answer cache does not purge provider-side prompt caches or CDN caches in front of your API.

notes.title: Observability, testing and failure patterns for budgets and caches
notes.html:
You operate these systems with numbers. Track them per tenant and per route.

Budget metrics: spend vs budget (percent), burn rate (spend per hour; project to end of period: projected = spent_so_far / elapsed_fraction), requests rejected by budget, degradation events by type, top spenders by feature and user, cost per request percentiles (p50, p99), reservation leak count (reserved minus settled for idle tenants).

Projection example: day 10 of a 30-day period, spent $900 of a $2,000 budget. Elapsed fraction = 10 / 30 = 0.333. Projected = 900 / 0.333 = $2,700, which is 35 percent over budget, so alert now rather than at 100 percent.

Cache metrics:

  • Hit rate = hits / (hits + misses), by route and tenant.
  • Tokens and dollars saved = hits times the average cost of a miss on that route.
  • False-hit rate from shadow sampling (section on correctness).
  • Staleness: age of served entries (p50, p95, max), and count of hits served after a source change (should be near 0).
  • Lookup latency and embedding latency; cold-start events after version bumps.
  • Eviction count and index size per tenant (memory pressure).

Memory and eviction. A vector store grows without limit unless bounded. Use per-tenant entry limits, an LRU or LFU policy (least recently or least frequently used items removed first), and TTL. Size estimate: 1,536 float32 dimensions = 1,536 * 4 bytes = 6,144 bytes per vector, plus answer text (say 2 KB) and metadata (0.5 KB), about 8.6 KB per entry. One million entries is about 8.6 GB before index overhead (HNSW graph overhead often adds a large fraction; verify for your store). That is why caches are bounded per tenant.

Testing strategy:

  1. Unit tests for the budget gate with concurrency: 1,000 threads reserve against a limit that fits 100; assert exactly 100 pass and the final spend is within the limit.
  2. A "poison" test set of near-miss pairs (enable/disable, annual/monthly, version numbers, different users) that must be misses; run it in CI whenever the threshold, embedding model or verifier changes.
  3. Tenant isolation tests: write an entry as tenant A with a unique canary phrase; query the same text as tenant B and assert a miss; do the same across permission groups and prompt versions.
  4. Invalidation tests: change a source document, then assert the dependent entry is gone within the agreed time, and test the lost-event path (TTL or read validation still catches it).
  5. Chaos: kill Redis, expire everything at once, fail the embedding service; confirm fail-open or fail-closed behaves as designed and that the LLM call path survives a cache outage (a cache must never be a hard dependency; wrap lookups in a short timeout, for example 50 ms, and treat a timeout as a miss).

Failure pattern catalogue.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Tenant sees another tenant's data missing tenant filter, post-filtering mandatory scope in client library, RLS, isolation tests
Wrong but confident answers on near-duplicate questions threshold too low, no verification calibrate, verifier, rule checks, shadow measurement
Stale answers after a policy edit TTL only event-driven invalidation plus version-in-key
Bill spikes after a release cold cache after version bump warm top queries, staged rollout
Idle tenant blocked as over budget leaked reservations release in finally, reconcile from usage log
Everything slow at the same minute synchronized expiry, stampede jittered TTL, single-flight
Hit rate drops overnight embedding or prompt version change, tenant-specific wording check version in scope, per-tenant tuning
Cache costs more than it saves low hit rate, expensive lookup measure break-even, disable on low-hit routes
Budget bypassed by background jobs metering only at gateway meter at the shared LLM client wrapper

Analogy (after): a shop's end-of-day till reconciliation. You do not trust that every sale was rung up correctly; you count the cash (usage log) against the register totals (Redis counters) and investigate differences.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting hit rate alone as the success metric, without false-hit rate and staleness.
  • Making the cache a single point of failure with no timeout.
  • Testing only the happy path, never concurrency or isolation.
  • Not budgeting for the cache's own memory, embedding calls and verifier calls.

notes.title: Putting it together: a reference design and a worked scenario
notes.html:
Combine the three pieces in one request path.

1. Authenticate -> tenant_id, user_id, roles -> acl_hash
2. Load tenant policy: plan, budget, cache_enabled, threshold, TTL
3. Rate limit (token bucket on requests and estimated tokens)
4. If route is cacheable and not personalised:
     scope = tenant|acl|model|prompt|index|embedding|lang
     embed query -> search scope -> candidate score
     score >= threshold AND guard checks pass (numbers, negation, verifier)?
        -> HIT: return, log saved cost, sample 2% for shadow comparison
5. MISS: reserve estimated cost (atomic). Over budget? -> degrade (smaller model / cache-only) or reject
6. Call LLM (single-flight on identical in-flight requests)
7. Settle actual cost; write usage event to the durable log
8. If cacheable: store answer with scope, sources (doc ids + versions), expires_at (TTL with jitter)
9. Events: document change -> targeted invalidation; deploy -> version bump + warm cache

Worked scenario. A SaaS vendor sells a help-desk chatbot to 200 companies. Tenant "Acme" is on a $2,000 monthly plan.

  1. Early in the period: Acme's burn rate is $190 per day. Projected spend = 190 * 30 = $5,700, versus $2,000. The projection alert fires on day 4 (when spent = $760, which is 38 percent of budget at 13 percent of the period), and the tenant admin gets a webhook. Investigation shows a script re-summarising the same 3,000 tickets every hour.
  2. The fix has three layers: an exact-match cache would have served the repeats (same input), a per-user daily cap stops one service account from spending more than $50 per day, and the 80 percent soft limit switches Acme's bulk route to the smaller model automatically.
  3. Separately, Acme updates its returns policy from 30 days to 14 days at 10:00. The CMS emits doc_changed(returns_policy). The reverse index finds 312 cached answers referencing that document and deletes them within seconds. A shadow check at 10:15 compares 20 sampled hits against fresh answers and finds 0 disagreements. Without event invalidation, those 312 entries would have kept saying "30 days" until their 7-day TTL expired, and customers would have been promised refunds the company no longer gives.
  4. Next, a user asks "How do I disable single sign-on?" and the cache holds an answer for "How do I enable single sign-on?" at cosine 0.96. The negation guard sees disable in one query and not the other, treats it as a miss, and the LLM answers correctly. A weekly report on guard-blocked hits shows which near-misses are common, and the team adds them to the poison test set.

Decision summary, how to choose:

  • Use exact cache first (safe, trivial), provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes, then semantic cache only for low-risk, repetitive, non-personalised routes.
  • Use version-in-key for anything that changes globally, events for document-level changes, TTL as a backstop, SWR for low-risk speed.
  • Use reserve-then-settle for hard caps, plain post-hoc accounting for soft caps and analytics.

Analogy (after): airport security with several lanes. Everyone is identified first (tenant), baggage is checked against rules (budget), frequent flyers with pre-checked status take the fast lane only if their credentials are current (cache hit with valid scope and version), and any change in the rules means the pre-check list is refreshed right away.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing the cache without saying which routes are excluded; strong answers name the exclusions (personalised, tool-dependent, time-sensitive, side-effecting).
  • Describing budgets without the degradation path and tenant communication.
  • Omitting the durable usage log and reconciliation.
  • Giving a single threshold number with no calibration method.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Multi-tenant LLM products need two protections: per-tenant budgets for money and fairness, and a carefully scoped cache for cost and latency. Both are correctness and security features, not just optimisations.
  • Meter every call (including retries, agent sub-calls and cancelled streams) using raw token counts and a versioned price table; output tokens usually cost more than input tokens. Budget in money or weighted credits.
  • Separate rate limits (speed), concurrency limits (parallelism) and budgets (total spend). Nest budgets by tenant, team, user and feature, with soft limits, graceful degradation (smaller model, lower max tokens, cache-only, batch queue) and hard ceilings.
  • Enforce hard budgets with atomic reserve-then-settle in a shared store such as Redis (Lua script, integer micro-dollars, release in finally), and keep a durable usage log as the system of record. Key counters by period so resets are automatic.
  • Use token buckets, weighted fair queues, priority lanes and backoff with jitter against noisy neighbours; remember the provider limit is shared by all tenants.
  • A semantic cache embeds the query, searches inside an exact scope, compares cosine similarity to a threshold and returns the stored answer. Break-even depends on the hit rate versus the lookup overhead.
  • Preventing wrong hits needs layers: hard scope filters (tenant, permissions, model, prompt, index, embedding model, language), no caching for personalised or tool-dependent answers, thresholds calibrated on labelled pairs, a verification stage (rules, reranker or small judge), and production shadow sampling to measure the false-hit rate.
  • Invalidate with the right tool per cause: TTL with jitter as a backstop, version-in-key for global changes (plan for the cold cache and warm it), event-driven deletion through a document-to-entry reverse index for targeted changes, validate-on-read when events can be lost, stale-while-revalidate for low-risk speed, and an emergency purge API.
  • Prevent stampedes with single-flight locks and jittered expiry; never let the cache be a hard dependency (short timeout, treat as miss).
  • Monitor spend burn rate and projection, hit rate, saved dollars, false-hit rate and staleness per tenant; test concurrency, near-miss pairs, isolation and invalidation paths in CI.
  • Numeric examples and thresholds in these notes are illustrations of the method; prices, limits, SDK method details and library features are fast-moving, so verify them in current provider and library docs.
